thresholds.scope: cash and/or bearer payment instruments (cheques, traveller's cheques, promissory notes, bills of exchange), in Rupiah or foreign currency, reaching or exceeding this amount in total
thresholds.authority: Indonesian Customs (Directorate General of Customs and Excise / Bea Cukai)
thresholds.mechanism: mandatory Customs Declaration via the applicable channel (All Indonesia integrated declaration for air/sea arrivals; Bea Cukai e-CD for land-border arrivals and outbound cash declarations); Government Regulation 99/2016

declaration.note: The declaration is triggered when the total value REACHES OR EXCEEDS IDR 100,000,000 (>=; 'IDR 100,000,000 or more'), or the equivalent in another currency, aggregating cash and bearer payment instruments in Rupiah or foreign currency, symmetric on entry and exit; failure to declare carries an administrative fine of 10% of the amount carried, up to a maximum of IDR 300,000,000. This is a customs / anti-money-laundering border-transparency declaration, NOT a currency import/export ceiling or a currency-control cap. It is distinct from three separate regimes that must not be conflated with it: the physical-Rupiah carriage rules (outbound Rupiah of IDR 100,000,000 or more requires prior Bank Indonesia permission; inbound is subject to a Customs authenticity examination), the foreign-banknote (UKA) carriage rules (IDR 1,000,000,000 or more restricted to Bank Indonesia-authorised entities), and the DHE SDA export-proceeds retention/placement regime.

exchange_controls.label: Free-foreign-exchange framework (Law 24/1999) with a floating Rupiah under a Flexible Inflation Targeting Framework, stated as a monetary-regime fact kept separate from controls; the reviewed official sources do not establish a single general exchange-control authorisation regime, but specific layered rules apply and are kept distinct — DHE SDA sector-specific export-proceeds retention/placement, non-resident Rupiah/foreign-exchange-market restrictions, the domestic Rupiah-use obligation, and the cross-border cash-declaration and Rupiah/UKA carriage regimes; absence of a located restriction is not evidence that none exists

bring_foreign_currency_in.label: Bringing currency in
bring_foreign_currency_in.text: Cash and/or bearer payment instruments (cheques, traveller's cheques, promissory notes, bills of exchange), in Rupiah or foreign currency, with a total value reaching or exceeding IDR 100,000,000 (or the equivalent in another currency), must be declared to Indonesian Customs (Bea Cukai) on arrival via the applicable Customs Declaration channel (the All Indonesia integrated declaration for air and sea arrivals, and the Bea Cukai e-CD for land-border arrivals), under Government Regulation 99/2016. Where the cash brought in is Rupiah of IDR 100,000,000 or more, its authenticity is examined by Customs. Foreign banknotes (Uang Kertas Asing, UKA) with a value of IDR 1,000,000,000 or more may be carried into the customs area only by Bank Indonesia-authorised entities (banks and licensed non-bank money changers), not by ordinary individuals, under BI Regulation 19/7/PBI/2017 as amended. Below these thresholds the reviewed sources establish no declaration or permission requirement.

source.section: PP 99/2016 — inbound declaration at or above IDR 100,000,000; Rupiah cash authenticity examination by Customs

take_foreign_currency_out.label: Taking currency out
take_foreign_currency_out.text: On departure the same IDR 100,000,000 customs declaration duty applies to cash and bearer payment instruments in Rupiah or foreign currency (Government Regulation 99/2016), filed through the Bea Cukai electronic Customs Declaration (e-CD), which is the channel Bea Cukai designates for outbound cash declarations. Physically carrying Rupiah banknotes of IDR 100,000,000 or more out of Indonesia additionally requires prior Bank Indonesia permission, a licensing requirement distinct from and not symmetric with the inbound treatment (inbound Rupiah of that amount is instead subject to a Customs authenticity examination). Carrying foreign banknotes (UKA) of IDR 1,000,000,000 or more out of the customs area is restricted to Bank Indonesia-authorised entities (BI Regulation 19/7/PBI/2017 as amended). The reviewed sources do not establish a separate general cap on the amount of foreign currency an individual may take out beyond these declaration and carriage rules.

source.section: PP 99/2016 — outbound declaration at or above IDR 100,000,000 (cash + bearer instruments), filed via the Bea Cukai e-CD

cash_declaration_threshold.label: Declaration threshold
cash_declaration_threshold.text: The declaration threshold is a total value that reaches or exceeds IDR 100,000,000 (or the equivalent in another currency) in cash and/or bearer payment instruments, in Rupiah or foreign currency, for a traveller entering or leaving Indonesia (Government Regulation 99/2016), declared to Bea Cukai through the applicable Customs Declaration channel (the All Indonesia integrated declaration for air and sea arrivals; the Bea Cukai e-CD for land-border arrivals and for outbound cash declarations). Failure to declare carries an administrative fine of 10% of the amount carried, up to a maximum of IDR 300,000,000, to the extent established by the reviewed sources. This customs / anti-money-laundering border declaration is distinct from the Bank Indonesia Rupiah-carriage and foreign-banknote (UKA) carriage licensing regimes and from the DHE SDA export-proceeds regime, and it is not a currency import or export cap.

source.section: PP 99/2016 — threshold IDR 100,000,000 or more (>=), cash + bearer instruments, Rupiah or foreign, entry and exit; administrative fine 10% up to IDR 300,000,000

exchange_controls.label: Exchange controls
exchange_controls.text: Indonesia does not operate a single general exchange-control authorisation regime in the reviewed sources; instead several distinct, layered regimes apply and must not be conflated: a customs declaration of cash and bearer instruments at or above IDR 100,000,000 (Government Regulation 99/2016); Bank Indonesia licensing and permission for physically carrying Rupiah banknotes (outbound of IDR 100,000,000 or more requires Bank Indonesia permission, while inbound of that amount is subject to a Customs authenticity examination) and foreign banknotes / UKA (IDR 1,000,000,000 or more restricted to authorised entities, BI Regulation 19/7/PBI/2017 as amended); the domestic Rupiah-use obligation with statutory exceptions (BI Regulation 17/3/PBI/2015); the DHE SDA export-proceeds retention and placement regime for natural-resource exporters (Government Regulation 36/2023 as amended through Government Regulation 21/2026); and foreign-exchange-market restrictions on Rupiah transactions with non-residents (BI Regulation 18/19/PBI/2016; BI Regulation 24/7/PBI/2022). The reviewed sources do not establish a general requirement of Bank Indonesia approval for capital transfers by residents, and they do not establish that Indonesia is 'fully liberalised' or has 'no controls'; absence of a located restriction is not evidence that none exists, and transaction-specific rules may apply.

source.section: Bank Indonesia — layered FX/currency regimes kept distinct; no single general exchange-control authorisation regime established; no 'no controls'/'fully liberalised' assertion

resident_holding_rules.label: Resident rules
resident_holding_rules.text: Residents (Penduduk) may hold and use foreign currency, while transactions conducted within Indonesian territory are generally required to be in Rupiah subject to statutory exceptions, including foreign-currency banking activities (BI Regulation 17/3/PBI/2015; statutory basis Law 7/2011 on Currency). The reviewed sources establish the Rupiah-use obligation and its exceptions but do not establish a general Bank Indonesia approval or quantitative limit on residents holding or operating foreign-currency accounts; the earlier on-file statement that residents face general BI limits or approval requirements for foreign-currency accounts is not supported by the located sources and is not asserted. Opening and operating bank accounts, including foreign-currency accounts, is governed by the general commercial-bank account-management rules (OJK Regulation POJK 24/2025) and by customer due diligence / know-your-customer under OJK Regulation POJK 8/2023; these govern the account-opening and account-administration process rather than establishing a residency-based entitlement. Under Indonesia's free-foreign-exchange framework (Law No. 24/1999), residents may hold and use foreign exchange, but the account-opening claim is not broadened beyond the located banking evidence, and account eligibility is not generalised beyond that evidence.

source.section: LAYER 1 — account management/opening: OJK POJK 24/2025 (Pengelolaan Rekening pada Bank Umum), general commercial-bank account-management/opening framework; governs account administration, not a residency-based entitlement

non_resident_rules.label: Non-resident rules
non_resident_rules.text: Non-residents (Bukan Penduduk) are subject to specific Bank Indonesia foreign-exchange-market restrictions in respect of Rupiah, including restrictions on Rupiah transfers abroad and on the provision of Rupiah credit or financing to non-residents, and limits on certain Rupiah transactions with non-residents (BI Regulation 18/19/PBI/2016; BI Regulation 24/7/PBI/2022 on the foreign-exchange market), subject to exceptions Bank Indonesia may allow. These are transaction- and market-level restrictions and do not by themselves establish a general non-resident bank-account-opening entitlement or prohibition. Account opening remains subject to the general commercial-bank account-management rules (OJK Regulation POJK 24/2025) and to customer due diligence / KYC (OJK Regulation POJK 8/2023). The located OJK sources prescribe customer-identification documentation, including foreign-citizen (Warga Negara Asing, WNA) documentation where applicable, but do not establish a general account-opening entitlement or prohibition based solely on Bank Indonesia resident/non-resident (Bukan Penduduk) status; foreign-citizen (WNA) status is a nationality concept and is not treated as synonymous with the BI non-resident (Bukan Penduduk) residency/economic-status concept. Account eligibility for non-residents therefore remains deliberately bounded and is not generalised beyond the located evidence. The earlier on-file claim that non-residents may transfer funds 'more freely' is not supported and is not asserted.

source.section: LAYER 1 — account management/opening: OJK POJK 24/2025 (Pengelolaan Rekening pada Bank Umum); no account-opening entitlement or prohibition based on BI resident/non-resident status established

banking_conversion_practicality.label: Banking & channels
banking_conversion_practicality.text: Foreign-exchange conversion is available through banks authorised to conduct foreign-exchange activities and through licensed non-bank money changers (Kegiatan Usaha Penukaran Valuta Asing Bukan Bank, KUPVA Bukan Bank), which require a Bank Indonesia licence and are limited to authorised foreign-banknote exchange and related activities (BI Regulation 18/20/PBI/2016). Any conditions or limits Bank Indonesia applies specifically to money changers are particular to those licensees and are not general limits on bank customers. Documentation and underlying-transaction requirements may apply to larger foreign-exchange transactions, and the availability of a particular currency, service or rate is not guaranteed by any institution.

source.section: PBI 18/20/PBI/2016 — KUPVA Bukan Bank licensing and authorised activities; money-changer conditions not generalised to bank customers

source_authorities.label: Bank Indonesia (BI) — central bank; monetary policy and the foreign-exchange framework

Bank Indonesia — Monetary function: Flexible Inflation Targeting Framework (Flexible ITF); the Rupiah exchange rate floats (Bank Indonesia adopted a free-floating system in 1997), with Rupiah exchange-rate stability pursued as part of monetary policy — kept separate from capital controls, account eligibility, DHE SDA, currency declaration and physical-cash carriage

Otoritas Jasa Keuangan (OJK) Regulation POJK No. 24 of 2025 — Account Management at Commercial Banks (Pengelolaan Rekening pada Bank Umum); the current general account-management / account-opening governance framework (standardised opening, closing, reactivation and account administration). Governs account management, not a residency-based account-opening entitlement or prohibition

declaration.note: Two parallel EUR 10,000 regimes administered through a single ADM declaration form: the EU external-border regime (Art. 3 Reg (EU) 2018/1672) and the Italian national-territory regime, which also covers intra-EU movements to or from other Member States (Art. 3 D.Lgs 195/2008). bring_foreign_currency_in.label: Bringing currency in

Where the traveller enters the European Union through Italy the obligation arises under Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2018/1672; where the traveller enters Italian national territory from another EU Member State it arises under Article 3 of Legislative Decree 195/2008. 'Cash' includes currency, bearer-negotiable instruments and gold used as a highly liquid store of value.

take_foreign_currency_out.label: Taking currency out
take_foreign_currency_out.text: Cash of EUR 10,000 or more taken out of Italy must be declared to the Italian customs authority (ADM) at the first border customs office. The obligation applies on leaving the European Union through Italy (Article 3, Regulation (EU) 2018/1672) and on leaving Italian national territory towards another EU Member State (Article 3, Legislative Decree 195/2008). The same cash categories apply; a declaration with inexact or incomplete information does not satisfy the obligation.

source.section: ADM Circular 12/2024 (p.1): exit — Article 3 Reg (EU) 2018/1672 (leaving the Union) and Article 3 D.Lgs 195/2008 (leaving national territory); EUR 10 000; first border customs office

cash_declaration_threshold.label: Declaration threshold
cash_declaration_threshold.text: The threshold for a mandatory declaration of accompanied cash carried by a traveller is EUR 10,000 or more. Two parallel regimes apply and are administered through a single ADM declaration form: Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2018/1672 for cash entering or leaving the European Union, and Article 3 of Legislative Decree 195/2008 for cash entering or leaving Italian national territory (including to and from other EU Member States). Unaccompanied cash sent by post, freight or courier is covered separately by Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2018/1672 (disclosure on the request of customs). Customs may require production of the cash and apply administrative seizure; specific penalty amounts are fixed by Legislative Decree 195/2008.

source.section: ADM Circular 12/2024 (p.1): EUR 10 000 or more; two parallel regimes (Art. 3 Reg (EU) 2018/1672 EU border; Art. 3 D.Lgs 195/2008 national territory) via a single declaration form

exchange_controls.label: Exchange controls
exchange_controls.text: Italy maintains no national exchange-control regime for capital movements or payments. Under Article 63 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, all restrictions on the movement of capital and on payments, between Member States and with third countries, are prohibited. This is not unconditional: the Treaty preserves exceptions, including measures on taxation and the prudential supervision of financial services and declaration procedures for administrative or statistical purposes (Article 65), the option to maintain certain restrictions on direct investment involving third countries (Article 64), and temporary safeguard measures (Article 66), alongside EU restrictive measures (sanctions). This capital-movement framework is separate from the EUR 10,000 cross-border cash-declaration regimes.

source.section: European Parliament, Fact Sheets on the EU — Free movement of capital: Article 63 TFEU prohibits all restrictions on the movement of capital and on payments (between Member States and with third countries); exceptions in Article 65 (taxation, prudential supervision, declaration procedures, public policy/security), Article 64 (third-country direct investment) and Article 66 (temporary safeguards)

resident_holding_rules.label: Resident rules
resident_holding_rules.text: Within the EU Treaty framework, general restrictions on capital movements and payments are prohibited (Article 63 TFEU), and no Italy-specific general prior-approval exchange-control regime applies to residents holding or transferring foreign currency. This does not guarantee that any given resident may open any particular foreign-currency account: holding and transferring funds remain subject to sanctions, anti-money-laundering and identity verification, taxation, reporting, prudential rules (Article 65 TFEU), and each supervised intermediary's own conditions.

source.section: European Parliament, Fact Sheets on the EU — Free movement of capital: Article 63 TFEU prohibits all restrictions on the movement of capital and on payments (between Member States and with third countries); exceptions in Article 65 (taxation, prudential supervision, declaration procedures, public policy/security), Article 64 (third-country direct investment) and Article 66 (temporary safeguards) — framework for resident foreign-currency holding; no Italy-specific prior-approval regime; Article 65 controls apply

non_resident_rules.label: Non-resident rules
non_resident_rules.text: Article 63 TFEU prohibits restrictions on capital movements and payments both between Member States and with third countries, so no general exchange-control restriction applies to non-residents holding accounts or transferring funds in Italy. This creates no entitlement to an account or service: onboarding, taxation, sanctions screening, anti-money-laundering and identity verification, reporting, and each institution's conditions apply, and the Treaty preserves certain third-country exceptions (Articles 64 and 65 TFEU).

source.section: European Parliament, Fact Sheets on the EU — Free movement of capital: Article 63 TFEU prohibits all restrictions on the movement of capital and on payments (between Member States and with third countries); exceptions in Article 65 (taxation, prudential supervision, declaration procedures, public policy/security), Article 64 (third-country direct investment) and Article 66 (temporary safeguards) — capital movements and payments with third countries covered; no entitlement to an account/service; Article 64-65 exceptions

Authorisation and supervision establish the regulatory routing; they do not guarantee that any particular institution offers a given currency, service or price. Access remains subject to each intermediary's onboarding, anti-money-laundering and identity verification, sanctions screening, and reporting requirements.

declaration.note: The declaration is triggered only ABOVE USD 10,000 (exceeding, not 'USD 10,000 or more'), aggregating cash, national or foreign checks, payment orders and other collectible documents; failure to declare carries a fine of 20%–40% of the excess (Ley Aduanera Art. 185 fr. VII). This is a customs currency-transparency declaration, not a currency-control cap, and is distinct from the anti-money-laundering controls and quantitative US-dollar cash-operation limits banks apply under Article 115 of the Ley de Instituciones de Crédito, from UIF AML reporting, and from the LFPIORPI domestic cash-payment limits.

exchange_controls.label: Free-floating exchange-rate regime set by the Comisión de Cambios (SHCP and Banco de México); the reviewed official sources do not establish a general foreign-exchange authorisation regime, with anti-money-laundering, US-dollar cash-operation, customs-declaration and any sectoral restrictions kept distinct

bring_foreign_currency_in.label: Bringing currency in
bring_foreign_currency_in.text: A traveller entering Mexico must file a mandatory customs declaration when the means of payment carried — cash, national or foreign checks, payment orders or any other collectible document, or a combination — exceed the equivalent of USD 10,000 in total (Ley Aduanera, Article 9), on the official form approved by the SAT. At or below that amount no declaration is required. The operational customs authority is the Agencia Nacional de Aduanas de México (ANAM). This customs declaration is distinct from the anti-money-laundering controls and cash-operation limits on US-dollar cash operations at banks.

source.section: Ley Aduanera Art. 9 — inbound: mandatory declaration when means of payment exceed USD 10,000; SAT-approved form; ANAM authority

take_foreign_currency_out.label: Taking currency out
take_foreign_currency_out.text: A traveller leaving Mexico must likewise file a mandatory customs declaration when the means of payment carried exceed the equivalent of USD 10,000 in total (Ley Aduanera, Article 9); the obligation is symmetric with entry. The reviewed official sources do not establish a Banco de México permission or export limit on physically carrying currency out of the country; the only monetary threshold on the traveller identified is the customs declaration duty. Anti-money-laundering controls and US-dollar cash-operation limits apply separately to cash operations conducted through banks.

source.section: Ley Aduanera Art. 9 — outbound: mandatory declaration when means of payment exceed USD 10,000 (symmetric with entry)

cash_declaration_threshold.label: Declaration threshold
cash_declaration_threshold.text: The customs declaration threshold is means of payment — cash, national or foreign checks, payment orders or any other collectible document, or a combination — exceeding the equivalent of USD 10,000 in total, for a traveller entering or leaving the country (Ley Aduanera, Article 9). It is a mandatory report to the customs authorities (ANAM) on the SAT-approved form, triggered only above USD 10,000; failure to declare carries a fine of 20% to 40% of the excess (Article 185, fracción VII). This border declaration is separate from three other regimes: anti-money-laundering controls and quantitative limits on US-dollar cash operations (Ley de Instituciones de Crédito, Article 115), UIF suspicious- and cash-transaction reporting, and the LFPIORPI domestic cash-payment limits.

source.section: Ley Aduanera Art. 9 (threshold: means of payment exceeding USD 10,000 in total, entry and exit; mandatory) and Art. 185 fr. VII (penalty)

exchange_controls.label: Exchange controls
exchange_controls.text: Mexico's foreign-exchange regime is free-floating and set by the Comisión de Cambios — the SHCP and Banco de México — under Article 21 of the Ley del Banco de México; the Comisión determines the exchange-rate regime and Banco de México sets the rules for determining the exchange rate (Ley Monetaria, Article 8). The reviewed official sources do not establish a general authorisation, permission or approval regime for buying, holding or transferring currency; this reflects the limits of the sources reviewed, not a positive finding that no sectoral or capital-movement restriction exists. The operative restrictions identified are of a different character and are kept distinct — anti-money-laundering controls and quantitative limits on US-dollar cash operations (Ley de Instituciones de Crédito, Article 115), the customs border declaration (Ley Aduanera, Article 9), and AML reporting. Whether any narrower sectoral or capital-movement restriction exists outside the reviewed sources is not established either way.

source.section: Ley del Banco de México Art. 21–22 — Comisión de Cambios sets the exchange-rate regime (free float). The reviewed sources do not establish a general FX authorisation regime

resident_holding_rules.label: Resident rules
resident_holding_rules.text: Under Banco de México Circular 3/2012, credit institutions may open peso (national-currency) deposit accounts to both natural and legal persons, with the lowest-tier and special-savings accounts reserved for natural persons. The reviewed official sources do not establish an unrestricted right for any resident to hold a foreign-currency (US-dollar) account: foreign-currency sight deposits payable in Mexico are available only to defined categories — natural persons domiciled in the northern 20-kilometre border strip or in Baja California and Baja California Sur, legal persons domiciled in national territory, and official representations of foreign governments and international organisations — while US-dollar transfer (SPID) accounts are opened only to legal persons domiciled in national territory. Banks also apply anti-money-laundering monitoring and reporting requirements to foreign-currency cash operations, together with quantitative daily and monthly limits on US-dollar cash operations for individual users differentiated by nationality, under the general provisions for Article 115 of the Ley de Instituciones de Crédito. Account opening remains subject to AML/KYC and each institution's own conditions; eligibility does not guarantee that any particular account will be opened.

source.section: Banco de México Circular 3/2012 — Art. 8 (peso deposit accounts open to personas físicas y morales; lowest-tier and special-savings accounts only personas físicas); Art. 45–46 (foreign-currency sight deposits: personas físicas domiciled in the 20 km northern border strip or Baja California / Baja California Sur; personas morales domiciled in territorio nacional; official foreign-government and international-organisation representations); US-dollar transfer (SPID) accounts only personas morales domiciled in territorio nacional. The reviewed sources do not establish a general resident right to a foreign-currency account. Current-compiled article numbers to be pinpoint-confirmed against the consolidated text

non_resident_rules.label: Non-resident rules
non_resident_rules.text: The reviewed official sources do not establish a general entitlement for non-residents to hold foreign-currency accounts in Mexico: eligibility for foreign-currency sight deposits and for US-dollar transfer (SPID) accounts is tied to domicile in national territory, so non-resident persons generally fall outside these categories, aside from official representations of foreign governments and international organisations. A separate peso-denominated deposit and prepaid-card regime exists for Mexican nationals whose place of residence is abroad. US-dollar cash operations are additionally subject to anti-money-laundering controls and to quantitative limits for individual users differentiated by nationality under Article 115 of the Ley de Instituciones de Crédito. Account opening remains subject to sanctions, anti-money-laundering and know-your-customer screening and each institution's requirements; there is no entitlement to any particular account or service.

source.section: Banco de México Circular 3/2012 Art. 45–46 — foreign-currency deposit eligibility keyed to domicile in territorio nacional (personas morales) or the northern border strip / Baja California (personas físicas), plus official foreign-government and international-organisation representations; US-dollar transfer (SPID) accounts only personas morales domiciled in territorio nacional. A distinct peso regime exists for Mexican nationals resident abroad. The reviewed sources do not establish general non-resident foreign-currency-account eligibility. banking_conversion_practicality.text: Currency conversion and cross-border payments in Mexico are provided through banks, and through casas de cambio and centros cambiarios authorised and supervised under Mexican law by the Comisión Nacional Bancaria y de Valores (CNBV) and Banco de México. These authorised intermediaries apply anti-money-laundering identification and controls on US-dollar cash operations under Article 115 of the Ley de Instituciones de Crédito, including quantitative limits on US-dollar cash operations for individual users differentiated by nationality; authorisation does not guarantee that any particular institution offers a given currency, service or price.

The fixed SAR/USD peg is a separate monetary-regime fact.

exchange_controls.label: Saudi riyal maintained at a fixed rate against the US dollar (SAR 3.75) by the Saudi Central Bank (SAMA) as a monetary-regime fact, kept separate from control posture; the reviewed official sources establish a licensed, SAMA-regulated foreign-exchange market (banks and money-exchange businesses) but do not establish a general exchange-control authorisation regime for buying, holding or transferring currency, and absence of a located restriction is not evidence that none exists — the AML border declaration, account-eligibility and any sectoral rules are kept distinct

bring_foreign_currency_in.label: Bringing currency in
bring_foreign_currency_in.text: A traveller entering Saudi Arabia must declare to ZATCA any currency (Saudi or foreign), bearer negotiable instruments, gold bullion, precious metals, gemstones or worked jewellery whose total value reaches or exceeds SAR 40,000 or the equivalent in another currency, using the prescribed declaration mechanism. Below that threshold no declaration is required. The declaration duty derives from Article 23/1 of the Implementing Regulation to the Anti-Money Laundering Law.

source.section: Art. 23/1 (amended, Umm Al-Qura) — primary legal locator: inbound written declaration when covered items reach or exceed (>=) SAR 40,000 or equivalent, under the prescribed form

take_foreign_currency_out.label: Taking currency out
take_foreign_currency_out.text: A traveller leaving Saudi Arabia must likewise declare currency, bearer negotiable instruments, gold bullion, precious metals, gemstones or worked jewellery whose total value reaches or exceeds SAR 40,000 or the equivalent (Article 23/1 of the Implementing Regulation to the Anti-Money Laundering Law); the obligation is symmetric with entry. The reviewed official sources do not establish a separate Saudi Central Bank permission or export cap on physically carrying currency out beyond this declaration duty.

source.section: Art. 23/1 (amended, Umm Al-Qura) — primary legal locator: outbound written declaration when covered items reach or exceed (>=) SAR 40,000 or equivalent (symmetric with entry), under the prescribed form

cash_declaration_threshold.label: Declaration threshold
cash_declaration_threshold.text: The declaration threshold is a total value reaching or exceeding SAR 40,000 (or the equivalent in another currency) in currency, bearer negotiable instruments, gold bullion, precious metals, gemstones or worked jewellery, for a traveller entering or leaving the Kingdom (Article 23/1 of the Implementing Regulation to the Anti-Money Laundering Law), declared to ZATCA through the prescribed mechanism. This anti-money-laundering border declaration is distinct from bank AML/KYC reporting and from SAMA's account-eligibility rules.

source.section: Art. 23/1 (amended, Umm Al-Qura) — primary legal locator establishing the current rule directly: threshold SAR 40,000 or equivalent, trigger 'reaches or exceeds' (>=), entry and exit, covered items (currency, bearer negotiable instruments, gold bullion, precious metals, gemstones and worked jewellery), written declaration under the prescribed form

exchange_controls.label: Exchange controls
exchange_controls.text: The Saudi Riyal is maintained at a fixed exchange rate against the US Dollar (SAR 3.75) by the Saudi Central Bank (SAMA); this is a monetary-regime fact and does not by itself establish the presence or absence of exchange or capital-movement controls. The reviewed official sources establish a licensed foreign-exchange market (banks and SAMA-licensed money-exchange businesses), account-eligibility conditions by customer category, a cross-border AML declaration regime and AML/KYC requirements; they do not establish a general exchange-control authorisation regime for buying, holding or transferring currency. Absence of a located restriction is not evidence that none exists, and narrower sectoral or transaction-specific rules may apply.

source.section: SAMA 'Affirms Commitment to Exchange Rate Policy' (5 Apr 2020) — SAR/USD peg at 3.75 as a monetary-regime fact only, kept separate from exchange-control posture; the peg is not used to infer convertibility, capital-account liberalisation, or absence of controls

resident_holding_rules.label: Resident rules
resident_holding_rules.text: Under SAMA's Account Opening Rules, bank customers may open accounts in any available foreign currency and deposit and withdraw in that currency; where the currency is unavailable, payment may be made in Saudi riyal. Eligibility to open and operate an account depends on the account-opening conditions for the customer's category and on AML/KYC requirements; the reviewed sources do not establish an unconditional right for any person to hold a particular account.

source.section: Account Opening Rules — customers may open foreign-currency accounts and deposit/withdraw in that currency, subject to category-based account-opening conditions and AML/KYC

non_resident_rules.label: Non-resident rules
non_resident_rules.text: Under SAMA's Account Opening Rules, banks may not open a Saudi-riyal account, a foreign-currency account, or any other account for non-Saudi, non-GCC natural persons who do not reside in Saudi Arabia unless written approval from the Ministry of Interior or the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is obtained through SAMA. Saudi citizens residing abroad and GCC nationals are addressed by their own account-opening rules within the same framework. The reviewed sources therefore do not support a general statement that non-residents may open or operate accounts freely; eligibility is category-specific and, for non-Saudi/non-GCC non-residents, conditional on the prescribed approval.

source.section: Account Opening Rules — banks shall not open SAR / foreign-currency / any account for non-Saudi, non-GCC natural persons not residing in the Kingdom without written MOI/MOFA approval through SAMA; distinct rules for Saudi citizens abroad and GCC nationals

banking_conversion_practicality.label: Banking & channels
banking_conversion_practicality.text: Currency conversion and transfers are available through licensed banks and SAMA-licensed money-exchange businesses, within their respective licensed scope. Any client conditions or limits that SAMA applies to money-exchange businesses are specific to those licensees and are not general limits on bank customers. Availability of a particular currency, service or price is not guaranteed by any institution.

source.section: Account Opening Rules — bank customers' foreign-currency accounts and conversion; category-based eligibility

SAMA Rulebook — Account Opening Rules (foreign-currency accounts; customer-category eligibility; non-Saudi/non-GCC non-resident written-approval requirement)

SAMA Rulebook — Rules Regulating Money Changing Business (SAMA Decision No. 4686, 1441H/2020; in force): licensing of money-changing business (Art. 6); permitted activities (Art. 11) — purchase, sale and trading of foreign currencies inside the Kingdom, and import/export of currencies for company/foreign-branch money changers; money transfers inside and outside the Kingdom permitted only to holders of valid SAMA licences at issuance (no new branches for that activity). Scope specific to money-exchange licensees; not general limits on bank customers

Implementing Regulation to the Anti-Money Laundering Law — Article 23/1 (amended traveller declaration: currency, bearer negotiable instruments, gold bullion, precious metals, gemstones and worked jewellery reaching or exceeding SAR 40,000 or equivalent, entry and exit, written declaration under the prescribed form), Umm Al-Qura official gazette

thresholds.scope: South African bank notes
thresholds.applies: taking out; unlimited within the Common Monetary Area
thresholds.authority: South African Reserve Bank (SARB); declared to SARS Customs
thresholds.mechanism: prior SARB authorisation required above this amount

thresholds.scope: 'excess currency' — any amount in rand, or foreign currency convertible to rand
thresholds.authority: South African Reserve Bank (SARB); declared to SARS Customs

declaration.note: Two distinct SARB exchange-control thresholds: the R25,000 rand-carrying limit on South African bank notes (unlimited within the Common Monetary Area, sourced to the SARS Departure page) and the R100,000 excess-currency rule covering rand or foreign currency convertible to rand (sourced to the SARS Travellers page). Separately, the traveller declaration — bank notes, foreign currency, securities and gold — is administered by SARS via an online form or the manual Traveller Declaration (TD-01). This R25,000 rand-carrying limit is a SARB exchange-control figure and is NOT the Currency and Exchanges Manual's R25,000 ADLA money-transfer cap.

exchange_controls.label: Current account largely liberalised; capital account subject to SARB exchange control administered through Authorised Dealers under the Currency and Exchanges Manual

bring_foreign_currency_in.label: Bringing currency in
bring_foreign_currency_in.text: Foreign currency may be brought into South Africa without limit. Travellers must declare the currency in their possession; the traveller declaration is administered by SARS through an online declaration form or the manual Traveller Declaration (TD-01). Any amount in excess of R100,000 — rand or foreign currency convertible to rand — is treated as excess currency under the Exchange Control Regulations and requires prior written permission from the SARB.

source.section: Import of currency — traveller declaration (online / TD-01); excess currency over R100,000 (rand or FC convertible to rand) requires SARB written permission

take_foreign_currency_out.label: Taking currency out
take_foreign_currency_out.text: South African bank notes may be taken out up to R25,000, and are unlimited only when travelling within the Common Monetary Area; carrying rand above R25,000 requires prior authorisation from the SARB. Currency in excess of R100,000, whether rand or foreign currency convertible to rand, requires written SARB permission. A traveller leaving South Africa must declare the currency in their possession to SARS Customs, which may search and seize currency under the Exchange Control Regulations.

source.section: Departure — SA bank notes up to R25,000 (unlimited within the CMA); above R25,000 requires prior SARB authorisation; Customs may search and seize under Exchange Control Regulations 3(3) and 3(6)

cash_declaration_threshold.label: Declaration threshold
cash_declaration_threshold.text: Two distinct thresholds apply and must not be conflated. First, the SARB rand-carrying limit: South African bank notes above R25,000 may not be taken out without prior SARB authorisation, and are unlimited only within the Common Monetary Area. Second, the SARB excess-currency rule: any amount, rand or foreign currency convertible to rand, in excess of R100,000 requires written SARB permission before entering or leaving. Separately, the traveller declaration — covering bank notes, foreign currency, securities and gold — is administered by SARS via an online form or the manual TD-01.

source.section: SARB rand-carrying limit — SA bank notes above R25,000 require prior SARB authorisation (unlimited within the CMA)

exchange_controls.label: Exchange controls
exchange_controls.text: South Africa maintains a floating exchange-rate regime with exchange controls administered by the SARB Financial Surveillance Department under the Exchange Control Regulations, 1961. Current-account transactions are largely liberalised; certain capital-account movements remain subject to controls, prior approval and reporting.

source.section: Exchange controls administered by SARB Financial Surveillance under the Exchange Control Regulations, 1961; current-account liberalised, capital-account controlled

resident_holding_rules.label: Resident rules
resident_holding_rules.text: South African residents transact foreign exchange through Authorised Dealers under the Currency and Exchanges Manual for Authorised Dealers. Resident individuals are accorded a single discretionary allowance of R2 million per calendar year and a foreign capital allowance of R10 million per applicant per calendar year; the foreign capital allowance and larger transfers are subject to the South African Revenue Service Tax Compliance Status (TCS) process. These two annual allowance limits may not be exceeded.

source.section: Single discretionary allowance — R2 million per calendar year (Authorised Dealer Manual section B.4)

non_resident_rules.label: Non-resident rules
non_resident_rules.text: Exchange controls on non-residents have been abolished, and qualifying non-resident income and securities proceeds are freely transferable. Non-residents transact through Non-resident Rand accounts and vostro accounts held by Authorised Dealers, and funds introduced from abroad may be retransferred. Certain transactions still require documentary evidence and settlement through approved channels.

source.section: Exchange controls on non-residents abolished; non-resident income and securities proceeds freely transferable; settlement via Non-resident Rand / vostro accounts

banking_conversion_practicality.label: Banking & channels
banking_conversion_practicality.text: Foreign-exchange conversion and cross-border transfers are handled by Authorised Dealers appointed by the SARB. Authorised Dealers perform customer due diligence under section 21 of the Financial Intelligence Centre Act, and all cross-border transactions are reported through the SARB Reporting System using the prescribed purpose codes.

source.section: Authorised Dealer customer due diligence under section 21 of the Financial Intelligence Centre Act

thresholds.scope: means of payment — foreign currency, Korean-won notes and checks — combined, exceeding this amount in total
thresholds.authority: Korea Customs Service
thresholds.mechanism: mandatory declaration (Traveler Declaration Form item no. 3; Certificate of Foreign Currency Declaration)

declaration.note: The declaration is triggered only ABOVE USD 10,000 (exceeding, not 'USD 10,000 or more'), aggregating foreign currency, Korean-won notes and checks; at or below USD 10,000 none is required. This Korea Customs border declaration is distinct from three separate regimes: Foreign Exchange Transactions Act capital-transaction and method-of-payment reporting (FETA Art. 16/18); foreign exchange banks' reporting of FX sales over USD 10,000 to the National Tax Service (FETA Art. 21); and KoFIU anti-money-laundering reporting.

exchange_controls.label: Current-account payments and receipts substantially liberalised; capital transactions and certain methods of payment or receipt subject to transaction-specific notification, permission or reporting under the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act (via foreign exchange banks, the Bank of Korea Governor, or MOEF as competent authority); the Korean won is not fully internationalised

bring_foreign_currency_in.label: Bringing currency in
bring_foreign_currency_in.text: A traveller bringing means of payment into South Korea — foreign currency, Korean-won notes and checks combined — exceeding USD 10,000 in total must file a mandatory declaration with the Korea Customs Service, marking item no. 3 of the Traveler Declaration Form and receiving a Certificate of Foreign Currency Declaration. At or below USD 10,000 no permission or declaration is required. This customs declaration is distinct from any Foreign Exchange Transactions Act reporting on capital transactions.

source.section: Korea Customs — inbound: means of payment exceeding USD 10,000 in total requires a mandatory declaration (Traveler Declaration Form item 3; Certificate of Foreign Currency Declaration); at or below USD 10,000 none required

take_foreign_currency_out.label: Taking currency out
take_foreign_currency_out.text: A traveller leaving South Korea must likewise file a mandatory Korea Customs declaration when means of payment exceed USD 10,000 in total. Separately, under the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act, capital-account transfers by residents may require transaction-specific notification or permission through a foreign exchange bank or the Bank of Korea Governor; that reporting is distinct from the customs border declaration.

source.section: Korea Customs — outbound: mandatory declaration when means of payment exceed USD 10,000

cash_declaration_threshold.label: Declaration threshold
cash_declaration_threshold.text: The Korea Customs declaration threshold is means of payment exceeding USD 10,000 in total — aggregating foreign currency, Korean-won notes and checks — for a traveller entering or leaving the country; it is a mandatory report to Customs (Traveler Declaration Form item no. 3, yielding a Certificate of Foreign Currency Declaration), not merely a document to produce if questioned, and it is triggered only above USD 10,000. This border declaration is separate from three other regimes: Foreign Exchange Transactions Act capital-transaction notification or permission, foreign exchange banks' reporting of FX sales over USD 10,000 to the National Tax Service, and KoFIU anti-money-laundering reporting.

source.section: Korea Customs — declaration threshold: means of payment (foreign currency + KRW notes + checks) exceeding USD 10,000 in total; mandatory report; triggered only above USD 10,000

exchange_controls.label: Exchange controls
exchange_controls.text: South Korea regulates foreign exchange through the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act, administered by MOEF and the Bank of Korea. The Act sets procedures in three areas — transaction type, payment and receipt, and method of payment and receipt. Current-account payments and receipts are substantially liberalised, while capital transactions involving large fund movements are subject to transaction-specific notification or permission through foreign exchange banks, the Bank of Korea Governor, or MOEF. The Korean won is not fully internationalised. This is a regulated framework — not an absence of exchange controls and not full liberalisation of the capital account.

source.section: BOK Foreign Exchange System — FETA three-area structure (transaction type; payment and receipt; method of payment and receipt); current liberalised, capital notification/permission; won not fully internationalised

resident_holding_rules.label: Resident rules
resident_holding_rules.text: South Korean residents may open and hold foreign-currency accounts — resident accounts and resident foreign currency trust accounts — through foreign exchange businesses registered under Article 8 of the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act. Capital transactions, which under Article 3 of the Act include deposits, lending, securities and overseas real estate, require advance reporting under FETA Article 18; certain methods of payment or receipt require reporting under Article 16; and some payments to foreign countries may require permission under Article 15. Depending on the transaction the report is made to a foreign exchange bank or the Bank of Korea Governor, and holding and transfer remain subject to sanctions, AML/KYC, tax and reporting requirements. This does not guarantee that any resident may open any particular account.

source.section: BOK Foreign Exchange System — resident foreign-currency accounts via foreign exchange banks; capital-transaction reporting

non_resident_rules.label: Non-resident rules
non_resident_rules.text: Non-residents may open and operate non-resident accounts through foreign exchange businesses registered under the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act — external accounts and non-resident foreign currency trust accounts for foreign-currency funds, and non-resident Korean-won accounts and non-resident free-transfer Korean-won accounts for won funds (Foreign Exchange Transactions Regulations Article 2-6-2). Certain transactions require transaction-specific reporting to a foreign exchange bank or the Bank of Korea Governor (for example FETA Article 18 capital transactions), and repatriation is not unconditional; account opening remains subject to sanctions screening, AML/KYC, tax and each institution's requirements. There is no entitlement to any particular account or service.

source.section: BOK Foreign Exchange System — non-resident accounts via foreign exchange banks; transaction-specific reporting; repatriation not unconditional

banking_conversion_practicality.label: Banking & channels
banking_conversion_practicality.text: Currency conversion and cross-border payments in South Korea are provided through foreign exchange banks and other institutions authorised under the Foreign Exchange Transactions Act within the Bank of Korea / MOEF framework. These authorised intermediaries apply the Act's notification, permission and reporting procedures according to transaction type; authorisation does not guarantee that any particular institution offers a given currency, service or price.

source.section: BOK — conversion and cross-border payments via foreign exchange banks and institutions authorised under FETA; notification/permission/reporting by transaction type; not a service/price guarantee

thresholds.scope: combined value of cash, negotiable instruments without a named payee, jewellery, and precious metals
thresholds.applies: travellers aged 18 and above, inbound and outbound
thresholds.authority: UAE Customs / Central Bank of the UAE

declaration.note: The trigger is a COMBINED declarable value across several asset categories, not cash alone, and applies to passengers aged eighteen and above.

exchange_controls.label: No per-transaction approval controls; supervisory posture around the US-dollar peg, current-account flows largely liberal

bring_foreign_currency_in.label: Bringing currency in
bring_foreign_currency_in.text: Inbound travellers may carry foreign currency without a legislated statutory cap analogous to rigid import licences. When the traveller carries currencies, cheque-like bearer forms, jewellery, or precious metals whose combined declarable valuation exceeds AED 60,000, UAE customs doctrine expects a declaration aligned with traveller-transparency publications and ICP-aligned digital facilitation at covered ports. Household members under eighteen are not ordinarily required to lodge a standalone declaration beyond inclusion on a guardian declaration where facts support that treatment. Omitting mandated declarations where threshold facts exist is prosecuted as customs evasion risk rather than a routine paperwork preference.

source.section: Inbound declaration mechanics

take_foreign_currency_out.label: Taking currency out
take_foreign_currency_out.text: Departure differs operationally from arrival even when headline policy remains permissive: travellers leaving still face the AED 60,000 combined declarable corridor for cash-like and jewellery categories, but the supervisory emphasis shifts to outbound reporting and AML monitoring on later bank or wire corridors. Capital repatriation of salaries, divestment receipts, or investment proceeds is ordinarily not withheld by denomination-specific quotas; compliance teams instead scrutinise sourcing and screening on higher-value corridors. Institutional channels therefore remain the pragmatic choice for sizeable movements that would otherwise collide with traveller-only declaration mechanics.

source.section: Outbound / departure reporting

cash_declaration_threshold.label: Declaration threshold
cash_declaration_threshold.text: Federal traveller declaration standards align on a combined AED 60,000 reporting trigger across cash, negotiable instruments without a named payee, jewellery, and precious metals for passengers aged eighteen and above. The measure is grounded in anti-money-laundering transparency rather than a permit to carry only up to that mark. Officials provide structured declaration forms plus, on selected crossings, interoperable electronic submission consistent with ICA/ICP public guidance. Accuracy matters because valuation disputes feed enforcement channels separate from benign tourist exchanges below reporting facts.

source.section: AED 60,000 combined traveller reporting trigger

exchange_controls.label: Exchange controls
exchange_controls.text: Administrative parlance distinguishes true exchange controls—mandatory approvals per transaction—from the Emirates' supervisory posture, which concentrates on peg maintenance through monetary instruments and regulated institutions while keeping current-account style flows largely liberal. Profit repatriation, services exports, and re-invoicing frameworks do not require pre-clearance dossiers analogous to guarded-capital regimes. Where tension appears, it is typically compliance-driven delays at bank level rather than sovereign denial of lawful conversion.

source.section: Central bank supervisory remit versus capital-control jurisdictions

resident_holding_rules.label: Resident rules
resident_holding_rules.text: UAE residents maintain AED and multicurrency deposits domestically subject to universal banking AML standards rather than nationality-based holding prescriptions. Everyday conversion between dirhams and majors occurs through authorised institutions where CBUAE licence classes govern who may run exchange counters versus full banking. Residents remitting abroad use SWIFT-like rails with institution-level checks; there is no parallel household foreign-currency ceiling published like hard exchange-control jurisdictions. Relationship managers still expect documentation on unusually large legacy cash deposits.

source.section: Residents' domestic and foreign currency services

non_resident_rules.label: Non-resident rules
non_resident_rules.text: Non-resident individuals and corporates open AED or foreign-currency accounts with documentation typical of international banking centres. Repatriation of operating profits, sale proceeds, or payroll savings is not administratively throttled by sovereign conversion permits in the classic sense, though banks apply sanctions screening and correspondent-bank constraints. Non-residents engaging in mainland commercial activity coordinate with licensing authorities separately from FX mechanics. Digital wallets and PSP partnerships expand retail access but inherit the same compliance obligations.

source.section: Opening accounts / non-resident access

banking_conversion_practicality.label: Banking & channels
banking_conversion_practicality.text: Liquidity for tourists and corporates flows through multinational banks, local champions, licensed exchange houses, and airport concessions with published boards. Payments rails include instant domestic transfers where supported and cross-border wires with correspondent cut-offs. Corporates leaning on treasury workstations integrate FX hedging externally while domestic spot needs are satisfied OTC. Operational friction concentrates on onboarding due diligence—not on statutory quotas—when aligning with FATF-aligned programmes.

source.section: Retail and corporate FX access pathways

declaration.note: Two thresholds by jurisdiction: Great Britain applies GBP 10,000 (or equivalent) on entering or leaving the UK; Northern Ireland applies EUR 10,000 (or equivalent) when travelling between NI and a non-EU country outside the UK. Both derive from UK anti-money-laundering legislation and are administered by HMRC through Border Force.

exchange_controls.label: No general exchange controls (fully liberalised for current and capital account)

bring_foreign_currency_in.label: Bringing currency in
bring_foreign_currency_in.text: Foreign currency and sterling may be freely imported. Declaration to Border Force is required when carrying cash of £10,000 or more into Great Britain, or €10,000 or more into Northern Ireland from a non-EU country outside the UK, or the equivalent in foreign currency. An advance declaration may be submitted online up to 72 hours before travel; declaration on arrival is also permitted.

take_foreign_currency_out.label: Taking currency out
take_foreign_currency_out.text: Residents and non-residents may freely export foreign currency and sterling. Declaration to Border Force is required when taking out cash of £10,000 or more from Great Britain, or €10,000 or more from Northern Ireland to a non-EU country outside the UK, or the equivalent in foreign currency. Non-residents may repatriate the full amount of currency declared on entry.

cash_declaration_threshold.label: Declaration threshold
cash_declaration_threshold.text: Great Britain (England, Scotland and Wales): cash of £10,000 or more, or its equivalent in foreign currency, must be declared to Border Force when entering or leaving the UK. Northern Ireland: cash of €10,000 or more, or its equivalent, must be declared when travelling between Northern Ireland and a non-EU country outside the UK. These thresholds apply to cash and specified monetary instruments including notes and coins, bearer bonds, and signed travellers' cheques; for Northern Ireland the obligation also covers money orders, gold coins, bullion, and prepaid cards. declaration.note: Transporting an aggregate exceeding USD 10,000 across the US border triggers a mandatory FinCEN Form 105 (CMIR) to CBP under 31 U.S.C. 5316 and 31 CFR 1010.340. This traveller border report is distinct from Bank Secrecy Act filings by financial institutions — Currency Transaction Reports (CTR) and Suspicious Activity Reports (SAR) — and from Foreign Bank Account Reports (FBAR); none of those is a traveller declaration.

bring_foreign_currency_in.label: Bringing currency in
bring_foreign_currency_in.text: Foreign currency and US dollars may be imported without limit or prohibition. Any person bringing more than USD 10,000 in aggregate (cash or monetary instruments) into the United States must file FinCEN Form 105 (CMIR) with a CBP officer at the port of entry.

take_foreign_currency_out.label: Taking currency out
take_foreign_currency_out.text: US dollars and foreign currency may be physically transported out without a maximum amount, but transporting more than USD 10,000 in aggregate currency or covered monetary instruments requires FinCEN Form 105.

cash_declaration_threshold.label: Declaration threshold
cash_declaration_threshold.text: The reporting threshold is USD 10,000. Under 31 U.S.C. 5316 and 31 CFR 1010.340, transporting an aggregate amount exceeding that figure across the US border triggers a mandatory Currency and Monetary Instrument Report (FinCEN Form 105) to CBP. This traveler border report is distinct from Bank Secrecy Act filings by financial institutions — Currency Transaction Reports (CTR) and Suspicious Activity Reports (SAR) — and from Foreign Bank Account Reports (FBAR); none of those is a traveler declaration.

source.section: 31 CFR 1010.340 — report of transportation exceeding USD 10,000 (official eCFR)

exchange_controls.label: Exchange controls
exchange_controls.text: The United States has a free-floating exchange-rate arrangement and, having accepted IMF Article VIII, maintains an exchange system free of restrictions on payments and transfers for current international transactions, with no multiple currency practices — except for restrictions maintained solely for the preservation of national or international security, notified to the IMF. This finding covers current international transactions; capital-account movements are governed separately under the OECD Code of Liberalisation of Capital Movements and the US reservation schedule.

source.section: IMF 2026 Article IV Informational Annex (CR 2026/076), Fund Relations → Exchange Rate Arrangements: free-floating; exchange rate determined freely in the FX market; Article VIII; no restrictions on payments/transfers for current international transactions; no multiple currency practices; security-reason exception (EBD 144-(52/51)) — current-account scope only; capital-account governed separately

resident_holding_rules.label: Resident rules
resident_holding_rules.text: The United States does not maintain a general exchange-control regime over residents' foreign-currency holdings: under the OECD Code of Liberalisation of Capital Movements, the US reservation schedule contains no general capital-movement reservation restricting residents' holding, conversion, transfer, or repatriation of foreign currency. Its reservations are limited to enumerated sectoral inward direct investment and a small-issues securities-registration carve-out for non-resident issuers. Account access remains subject to sanctions, AML/KYC, tax, information-reporting, and prudential requirements.

source.section: OECD Code of Liberalisation of Capital Movements, Annex B, United States reservation schedule (page 134). The US lodges reservations only on List A, I/A direct investment in enumerated strategic sectors and List A, IV/B1-B2 (small-issues securities-registration for non-resident issuers); no general capital-movement reservation restricts residents' holding, conversion, transfer, or repatriation. Institutional secondary evidence.

non_resident_rules.label: Non-resident rules
non_resident_rules.text: For non-residents, the US schedule under the OECD Code of Liberalisation of Capital Movements contains no general reservation restricting ordinary transfer or repatriation; the recorded reservations concern enumerated inward-investment sectors and limited securities-registration treatment for non-resident issuers. This does not entitle every non-resident to every bank account or service: onboarding remains subject to sanctions screening, AML/KYC, information-reporting and withholding, and each institution's requirements.

source.section: OECD Code of Liberalisation of Capital Movements, Annex B, United States reservation schedule (page 134). The recorded reservations concern enumerated inward-investment sectors and small-issues securities-registration for non-resident issuers; no general reservation restricts ordinary non-resident transfer or repatriation. Institutional secondary evidence.

banking_conversion_practicality.label: Banking & channels
banking_conversion_practicality.text: Ordinary currency conversion and cross-border payments operate through regulated US financial institutions and money-services businesses, subject to BSA/AML, sanctions, tax, reporting, and institution-specific controls. Currency dealers or exchangers and money transmitters are money services businesses that must register with FinCEN under the Bank Secrecy Act and maintain applicable compliance programs.

source.section: FinCEN — Money Services Business (MSB) Registration. Establishes that currency dealers/exchangers and money transmitters are money services businesses that must register with FinCEN (Treasury) and comply with Bank Secrecy Act obligations — the claim-specific source for the regulated-institution routing of ordinary currency conversion and cross-border payments. Not sourced from the OECD absence of reservations.
